items.item: The four-way comparison (plain loop, multiprocessing, async, native engine) runs on the identical synthetic feed in one process, so the comparison is apples-to-apples rather than four separately-run, differently-sized benchmarks

at.step: Reveal: the lab — all four ways, measured together for real

items.item: Async is measured honestly as slower than the plain loop on this CPU-bound local-parsing workload, not merely 'no faster' — the topic does not soften a result that contradicts the chapter's earlier async win, since that win was for a different kind of workload entirely

at.step: Reveal: the lab — all four ways, measured together for real

items.item: The tracemalloc measurement went through a real correction during this build: an initial version compared post-call live block counts and got a backwards result, fixed by reading tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()'s own peak instead — documented as a finding, not silently rewritten away

at.step: Reveal: tracemalloc, quoted and measured

items.item: The py-spy attach is checked against the real subprocess's own actual function name appearing in the dump output, not merely that the dump command exited without an error

at.step: Reveal: the lab — py-spy attaching to a live process, for real

items.item: PEP 768 (3.14) and profiling.sampling (3.15) are both confirmed absent from this sandbox's CPython 3.13.16 by direct import/attribute checks, not assumed absent from the version number, and perf is confirmed absent by checking for the actual command rather than assumed
